newsitem.title: USA: Bonds funds not so boring.
newsitem.headline: Bonds funds not so boring.

text.p: Investors fixated on the stock market's big gains are ignoring this amazing fact: Long-term government bond funds have delivered 9.4 percent annual returns during the past decade -- a 5.7 percent annual return after inflation.
Not bad for an investment that some investors consider incapable of keeping pace with rising prices.
Yet investors are ignoring bond funds. According to Morningstar Investor, stock funds since 1994 have taken in $270 billion in new assets, while bond funds have suffered redemptions.

To be sure, investors who have bet on stocks over bonds during the past two or three years have been well rewarded. The average stock fund has gained 19.9 percent annually since 1994 vs. 6.2 percent for the typical government bond fund.

What's more, bonds remain a bit of a dark horse to win the investment sweepstakes going forward. The strong economy and low inflation bode well for stocks, and many observers worry that the Federal Reserve will boost interest rates and send bond prices lower.

But bond prices already reflect some of those factors. As a result, many bond funds offer attractive yields that could bolster the performance of your portfolio no matter what happens to the stock or bond markets. No wonder some bargain hunters who find stock prices overblown are starting to prospect for deals in the bond market.

If you are tempted to join them, follow these guidelines: Stay with your long-term strategy. Don't abandon your stock market investments even if you think stocks are too pricey. After all, stocks looked expensive to many intelligent people two years ago, and they got out then -- to their lasting regret.

A modest stake in bonds -- say 20 percent to 30 percent -- is plenty for most investors. Bonds are not without risk. When interest rates climb, long-term bonds and funds that hold them can suffer significant losses.

And funds that hold "high-yield" bonds, also known as junk bonds, can be risky as well. These funds hold bonds issued by companies in mediocre or downright bad financial condition. Such bonds' prices can decline sharply when economic weakness calls into question the issuers' ability to pay interest and principal they owe to their bondholders.

The best response to those risks is to diversify your bond holdings. If you own funds with long-term or high-yield bonds, make sure that you also invest in funds that hold investment-grade bonds with solid credit ratings and relatively short maturities.

In fact, some evidence suggests that funds investing in intermediate-term bonds, those that mature in roughly three to seven years, can offer better returns than riskier long-term funds. One solid intermediate bond fund is Harbour Bond (800-422-1050; $2,000 minimum investment; no load). Manager Bill Gross recently invested 94 percent of the portfolio in investment-grade bonds, including 80 percent in AAA issues.

Another option is Pegasus Bond (800-688-3350; $1,000 minimum; no load), which recently invested 43 percent of its portfolio in bond issues by the U.S. Treasury and government agencies. The fund has gained 7.7 percent annually during the past five years vs. 6.9 percent for the typical intermediate-term bond fund.

Watch fund expenses. A well-run stock fund may be able to make up for high annual expenses it charges shareholders. But even the best managed bond funds have a hard time justifying fees that are out of line with the competition. The reason: There are fewer ways to generate an extra dollop of return in the bond market -- and most of those methods are pretty risky.

Worse, some high-expense bond funds will take on those risks to try and make up for the fees they charge investors. Otherwise, their yield looks unattractive. For example, a fund manager might invest in high-yield bonds or long-term issues to get a higher payout, exposing investors to the risk of capital losses that could make their fund an even worse bargain in the long run.

Bond funds offered by Vanguard generally are distinguished by their low expense ratios. Among them: Vanguard High-Yield Corporate (800-662-7447; $3,000 minimum; no load), which invests in corporate debt with relatively low credit quality. The fund's expense ratio is only 0.3 percent, compared with 1.4 percent for the typical high-yield fund.

Vanguard GNMA (800-662-7447; $3,000 minimum; no load) also features an attractive expense ratio -- 0.3 percent vs. 1.2 percent for the fund's typical competitor. The fund, which invests in mortgage securities, has gained 9 percent annually during the past 10 years vd. 7.7 percent for the typical intermediate-term government bond fund.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a free-lance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
